alt: Causes of the First World War in three columns. Long-term: the two alliance blocs, colonial rivalry, arms build-up and Balkan nationalism. Short-term: the July 1914 ultimatum, Austria-Hungary’s declaration of war on Serbia and mobilisation. Trigger: the assassination of Franz Ferdinand on 28 June 1914. The alliances link them into a general war.
caption: Sort causes by timescale, then explain how they connect: that shows causality.

alt: A loop: state A arms to feel safe, so state B feels less safe and arms too, so state A feels less safe and arms again. Both end up less secure.
caption: Arming for safety can make everyone less safe.

alt: A chain: the First World War ends; the Treaty of Versailles of 28 June 1919 limits the German army to 100,000 men and blames Germany in Article 231; resentment helps the Nazis win support; Germany invades Poland on 1 September 1939 and the Second World War in Europe begins.
caption: Versailles was a consequence of one war and a cause of the next.

alt: Sixty squares stand for fictional Norland’s 6.0 million people. Fifteen are internally displaced (1.5 million) and nine were refugees (0.9 million), of whom six returned and three remain abroad. In total 40% were displaced, and 66.7% of refugees returned within two years.
caption: Two in five lost their homes; two-thirds of refugees came back within two years.

after: ## From the League of Nations to the United Nations
alt: The Security Council, with five veto-holding permanent members and ten elected members, can act under Chapter VI, peaceful settlement, or Chapter VII, sanctions and military force. Peacekeeping sits between them and needs consent. Korea in 1950 and Kuwait in 1990 were peace enforcement under Chapter VII.
caption: From persuasion to enforcement: peacekeeping sits in between, and the veto can block it all.

alt: Three principles: consent of the main parties, impartiality, and no use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Rwanda in 1994 and Srebrenica in 1995 show their limits when one side targets civilians.
caption: Consent, impartiality and minimal force keep a ceasefire, but cannot stop a side bent on killing.

alt: Four stages from An Agenda for Peace (1992): preventive diplomacy, peacemaking, peacekeeping and post-conflict peacebuilding. Peacekeeping mainly secures negative peace, the absence of fighting; peacebuilding aims at positive peace, where causes are addressed, using tools such as DDR, rebuilt courts and police, elections and transitional justice.
caption: Stopping the fighting is negative peace; addressing its causes is positive peace.
